action_requirements.intro: Part A lists the questions for management that remain after the analysis above; Part B lists the documents and data that evidence them. Records such as the cap table, management accounts and agreements are normally private: they are requested as standard diligence, not because their absence from public sources is a concern.

items.text: Performance of the current product under operating conditions: reliability, performance and usage data.
items.why: Product maturity rests on company statements; operating data shows whether the product performs at customer conditions.

items.text: Certification or qualification required for customer operation, its current status and what remains.
items.why: Determines when the product can be sold and used.

items.text: What is protected: patents or applications filed, and ownership of the core technology.
items.why: No patent position is established; defensibility depends on what the company owns and can protect.

items.text: Whether each founder works full-time for the company, given other current roles listed in public profiles (Jasper Deprez and Sanjay Vijendran), and any arrangements with those entities.
items.why: Delivery depends on a committed founding team; outside roles can also create related-party interests.

items.text: Current headcount by function and the key hires planned.
items.why: Shows whether the team can deliver the next milestones.

items.text: Customer discovery to date: organisations engaged, design partners, and any letters of intent or pilots under discussion.
items.why: At pre-seed the first sign of demand is engagement from the intended buyers.

items.text: Which segment and geography the company is prioritising - among data center operators, critical infrastructure operators, defence installations and other segments - why that one first, and how many qualifying sites or customers it counts there.
items.why: Research lists several target segments; the first one sets the sales cycle, reference customers and capital need.

items.text: The buying process in the target segment: budget owner, decision-makers, procurement steps and time from first contact to order.
items.why: The buying cycle sets how fast revenue can follow.

items.text: How much revenue is recurring rather than project-based, and the margin on each.
items.why: Project revenue scales with headcount unless it becomes recurring.

items.text: Current cash, monthly burn and runway, and the capital needed to reach the next technical and commercial milestones.
items.why: For a capital-intensive business, runway against the delivery timetable sets the size and timing of the next raise.

items.text: Current fundraising: amount sought, capital already committed, use of funds, and the technical and commercial milestones it is meant to reach.
items.why: Links the investment to specific milestones.

items.text: Alternatives actually weighed in customer discussions to date (for example continuing with terrestrial grid connection and diesel generation, or direct alternatives such as Space Solar), why the customer chose or would choose the company, what would stop a competitor replicating the offering, and any comparative cost or performance evidence.
items.why: Only buyer decisions show which alternatives compete; public research shows the field, not the customer's shortlist.

items.text: Ownership of the company: founders' shareholdings, option pool, founder vesting, and rights attached to the 2026 financings.
items.why: Determines founder incentives and the rights a new investor would rank alongside.

items.text: The legal entity behind the company - registered name, jurisdiction and registration number - and that it is active.
items.why: Financing, contracts and intellectual property attach to a specific legal entity.

profile.text: The arena, as research frames the job: “Provide reliable continuous electricity to hard-to-reach operations without dependable terrestrial grid access” - for enterprise customers - a vSET analytical frame. Research identifies 1 direct competitor - Space Solar; 3 other alternatives; customers' current way: Terrestrial grid connection and diesel generation (reported, not established). blocks: TerraSpark is developing space-based solar power systems. Its offering includes space-based solar power systems and wireless power transmission systems. It targets data center operators, critical infrastructure operators and defence installations, among other segments, with Luxembourg and Europe as named markets. The revenue model is project-based, sold to enterprise customers.

TerraSpark is a Pre-Seed-stage company, founded in 2025, based in Luxembourg. In March 2026 it stated funding would support initial pilot applications and live tests of its space-based solar technology. No customer commitment has been disclosed yet; the commercial case rests on the product and the need it addresses. It has completed one financing in 2026. The company is led by its three-person founding team (CEO).

blocks: It is developing developing space-based solar power systems, combining space-based solar power systems and wireless power transmission systems into one offering.
TerraSpark operates in upstream R&D and system integration, developing orbital generation and wireless transmission systems before delivering power to enterprise customers.
What may be harder for alternatives to replicate is proprietary technology / know-how and system integration, which depend on execution rather than on protected technology alone.

In March 2026 it stated funding would support initial pilot applications and live tests of its space-based solar technology. March 2026: TerraSpark was reported to be targeting an orbital technology demonstrator in 2027 and first space-to-Earth power transmission in 2028. The next meaningful step is use by paying customers.

The system combines four elements: orbital solar arrays capture sunlight; radio-frequency transmitters wirelessly deliver power; remote receivers or rectennas convert radiowaves into electricity; satellites, ground infrastructure, and control systems integrate the end-to-end system. According to the company: develops modular orbital solar generation and precisely directed RF wireless power transmission.
Cheaper launches and reusable spacecraft enable orbital demonstrations; example: planned 2027 demonstrator. TerraSpark's offering is built on this progress.

No patent position is established for TerraSpark; whether its software, data and algorithms are protected by patents, held as trade secrets or owned jointly with research partners requires confirmation.

sections.title: Market opportunity

blocks: Customers who need to provide reliable continuous electricity to hard-to-reach operations without dependable terrestrial grid access choose between continuing with their current way of working (terrestrial grid connection and diesel generation), adjacent automated systems (Aetherflux), like-for-like systems (Space Solar), extensions of incumbent suppliers' offerings (Rolls-Royce) and in-house builds or systems-integrator projects (Thales Alenia Space). Space Solar offers a directly comparable solution.

Space Solar could capture European utility, infrastructure, or government attention for the same future orbital-electricity procurement.
Rolls-Royce could retain an industrial or defence account by extending conventional power-generation infrastructure rather than adopting TerraSpark’s orbital system.
A government or utility-led programme could commission Thales Alenia Space to assemble a bespoke orbital power system instead of selecting TerraSpark.
